The Jacobian Conjecture
fails for pseudo-planesThanks: Research project partially funded by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Republic of Poland, Iuventus Plus grant no. 0382/IP3/2013/7

Adrien Dubouloz Address: IMB UMR5584, CNRS, Univ. Bourgogne Franche-Comté, F-21000 Dijon, France. Email address: adrien.dubouloz@u-bourgogne.fr and Karol Palka Address: Institute of Mathematics, Polish Academy of Sciences, Śniadeckich 8, 00-656 Warsaw, Poland Email address: palka@impan.pl
Abstract.

A smooth complex variety satisfies the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture if all its étale endomorphisms are proper. We study the conjecture for ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic surfaces of negative Kodaira dimension. We show that GG-equivariant counterexamples for infinite group GG exist if and only if G=ℂ∗G=\mathbb{C}^{*} and we classify them relating them to Belyi-Shabat polynomials. Taking universal covers we get rational simply connected ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-surfaces of negative Kodaira dimension which admit non-proper ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariant étale endomorphisms.

We prove also that for every integers r≥1,k≥2r\geq 1,k\geq 2 the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic rational hyperplane u⁡(1+ur​v)=wku(1+u^{r}v)=w^{k}, which has fundamental group ℤk\mathbb{Z}_{k} and negative Kodaira dimension, admits families of non-proper étale endomorphisms of arbitrarily high dimension and degree, whose members remain different after dividing by the action of the automorphism group by left and right composition.

Key words and phrases: 
Jacobian Conjecture, Q-homology plane, pseudo-plane, étale, equivariant, endomorphism, group action, Belyi map, Shabat polynomial

1. Main result

The Jacobian Conjecture asserts that if an algebraic endomorphism of the complex affine space 𝔸n=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn])\mathbb{A}^{n}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]) has an invertible Jacobian then it is an isomorphism. The conjecture is open and hard, even for n=2n=2. One of the ideas which may contribute to our understanding of it is to study the problem in a broader class of varieties. A general form of the conjecture has been proposed by M. Miyanishi.

Definition 1.1 (Generalized Jacobian Conjecture).

A smooth complex variety satisfies the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture if all étale endomorphisms of that variety are proper.

Unless the topological Euler characteristic of the variety is zero, properness is equivalent to the invertibility of the endomorphism (see Lemma 2.15), so for affine spaces the conjecture is equivalent to the original Jacobian Conjecture. The Generalized Jacobian Conjecture has been studied for certain classes of algebraic varieties, see Miyanishi’s lecture notes [Miy03] for a good introduction to the subject. It holds for quasi-projective varieties of log general type due to a result of Iitaka (see Lemma 2.15(4)) and it holds for curves by [Miy85]. For surfaces there are many positive partial results, see [Miy85], [MM02], [KM05], [MM06], [Miy06], [GM08]. But the most intriguing question, which is in fact the main motivation, is whether the conjecture holds for varieties similar to affine spaces, similar in the sense of having the same logarithmic Kodaira dimension or the same, i.e. trivial, rational homology groups. We restrict our attention to the intersection of these two classes in dimension two, that is, to ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes of negative Kodaira dimension. Similarly to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}, they all admit an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} (hence are rational, see Proposition 2.9). The only ℤ\mathbb{Z}-homology plane in this class is the affine plane 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} ([Miy01, 3.4.3.1]). As expected, the difficulty of the problem increases as we decrease the complexity of the fundamental group of the surface. Gurjar-Miyanishi [GM99, §6] argued that the conjecture holds if π1\pi_{1} is non-cyclic, but later Miyanishi noticed that the proof is wrong in case the fundamental group is ℤ2∗ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\mathbb{Z}_{2} and he found a counterexample of degree 22 in that case (see Proposition 2.10). In Section 3C we construct étale endomorphisms of every positive degree on Miyanishi’s surface.

The question for ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes of negative Kodaira dimension which have cyclic fundamental groups, called pseudo-planes, remained open. These surfaces are geometrically and topologically the most similar ones to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}, and hence the Jacobian Conjecture for them is of biggest interest. Our main result is that the conjecture fails for many of them, i.e. that their étale endomorphisms do not have to be proper. Surprisingly, this is so even if we impose an additional restriction that we look only for counterexamples invariant with respect to an effective action of an infinite algebraic group. In case a smooth complex variety comes with some effective algebraic action of a group GG then we say that it satisfies the GG-equivariant Generalized Jacobian Conjecture if all GG-equivariant étale endomorphisms of that variety are proper.

Let k,rk,r be positive integers. The smooth affine surface

(1.1) S~(k,r)={xry=zk−1}⊆Spec(ℂ[x,y,z])\tilde{S}(k,r)=\{x^{r}y=z^{k}-1\}\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z])

is simply connected (see Example 2.11) and for every a∈{1,2,…,k}a\in\{1,2,\ldots,k\} coprime with kk it admits a free ℤk\mathbb{Z}_{k}-action ε∗a(x,y,z)=(ε​x,ε−r​y,ε−a​z)\varepsilon*_{a}(x,y,z)=(\varepsilon x,\varepsilon^{-r}y,\varepsilon^{-a}z), where we identify ℤk\mathbb{Z}_{k} with the group of kk-th roots of unity (ℤ1≅{1}\mathbb{Z}_{1}\cong\{1\}). The quotient surface, denoted by S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a), is a pseudo-plane with fundamental group ℤk\mathbb{Z}_{k} and the hyperbolic ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action λ⋅(x,y,z)=(λ​x,λ−r​y,z)\lambda\cdot(x,y,z)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-r}y,z) descends to it. Masuda and Miyanishi [MM06] characterized the surfaces S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a), k,r≥2k,r\geq 2, as the only pseudo-planes with a hyperbolic ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action which admit a unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. We use this result to show the following reduction.

Theorem A.

Let SS be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane of negative Kodaira dimension with an effective action of an infinite algebraic group GG. The GG-equivariant Jacobian Conjecture holds for SS unless G=ℂ∗G=\mathbb{C}^{*} and SS is ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariantly isomorphic to some pseudo-plane S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a) for some k,r≥2k,r\geq 2 and a∈{1,2,…,k−1}a\in\{1,2,\ldots,k-1\} coprime with kk.

In the exceptional cases we obtain a classification (see Theorem D for a stronger and more detailed result).

Theorem B.

Let k,r≥2k,r\geq 2 be integers and let a∈{1,…,k−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\} be coprime with kk. The ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-pseudo-plane S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a) admits a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariant étale endomorphism of degree dd (hence non-proper for d>1d>1) if and only if

(1.2) d≡1modk⁡(r−1)​ or ​k|r,a=1​ and ​d≡rmodk⁡(r−1).d\equiv 1\mod k(r-1)\text{\ \ \ or\ \ \ \ }k|r,\ a=1\text{\ and \ }d\equiv r\mod k(r-1).

In particular, the ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariant Generalized Jacobian Conjecture fails for every S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a), k,r≥2k,r\geq 2 and hence for every finite cover of it.

The counterexamples we construct are closely related to polynomial Belyi maps, called Shabat polynomials, which we use to give explicit formulas, see Section 4. Since the conjecture (even in the ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariant version) fails for the surfaces S~​(k,r)\tilde{S}(k,r), k,r≥2k,r\geq 2, which are the universal covers of S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a), by taking a product with 𝔸n−1\mathbb{A}^{n-1} we obtain the following important result. Up to our knowledge these are the first simply connected rational counterexamples in the literature (cf. Remark 4.2).

Corollary 1.2.

For every positive integer nn there exists a smooth affine variety 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}-fibered over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} (hence rational and of negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension) which is simply connected and for which the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture fails.

The counterexamples in Theorem B are discrete in nature. However, we observe that the situation changes if we do not insist on ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariance. The following result shows that, although pseudo-planes are arguably the surfaces most similar to the affine plane, the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture for many of them fails very strongly.

Theorem C.

Let r¯≥1,k≥2\bar{r}\geq 1,k\geq 2 and let S=S⁡(k,k​r¯,1)S=S(k,k\bar{r},1) be a pseudo-plane as above. Then for every integer N≥0N\geq 0 there exist arbitrarily high-dimensional families of non-proper étale endomorphisms of SS of degree k⁡(N⁡(r¯​k−1)+r¯)k(N(\bar{r}k-1)+\bar{r}) such that all members of the family are different, even after dividing by the action of the automorphism group of SS by left and right composition.

We note that the surface S⁡(k,r¯​k,1)S(k,\bar{r}k,1) is isomorphic to the hypersurface u⁡(1+ur¯​v)=wku(1+u^{\bar{r}}v)=w^{k} in 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} and all counter-examples are given by explicit formulas. For instance, for the pseudo-plane S(2,2,1)≅{u(1+uv)=w2}S(2,2,1)\cong\{u(1+uv)=w^{2}\}, which has fundamental group ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, the formulas for the families from Theorem C are written in Example 5.7. We hope that our counterexamples could serve as a testing area for other researchers interested in the Jacobian Conjecture.

Finally, we note that boundaries of minimal log smooth completions of our counterexamples (which are rational trees, due to ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclicity) all contain a branching component, i.e. they are not chains. The ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes which admit a completion by a chain of rational curves constitute the most important remaining class to study. By [MM03, Theorem 3.4] and [Giz71] such surfaces are isomorphic to S⁡(k,1,a)S(k,1,a) for some k≥1k\geq 1 and a∈{1,…,k−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\} coprime with kk. In particular, Theorem A implies that they admit no GG-equivariant counterexamples for infinite groups GG. Via Lemma 2.16 it is enough to study the question for their universal covers.

Question 1.3.

Does the Jacobian Conjecture hold for S~(k,1)={xy=zk−1}\tilde{S}(k,1)=\{xy=z^{k}-1\}, k≥1k\geq 1?

Note that S~​(k,1)\tilde{S}(k,1) is a smooth simply connected surface admitting an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} (hence rational and of negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension) and that S~​(1,1)≅𝔸2\tilde{S}(1,1)\cong\mathbb{A}^{2}.

2. Preliminaries

We work with complex algebraic varieties.

2A. Branched covers of curves.

By a curve we mean an irreducible reduced variety of dimension one. Recall that, as a consequence of the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture holds for curves (see [Miy85, Lemma 1]).

Lemma 2.1 (GJC for curves).

Every dominant morphism between curves of equal topological Euler characteristic is finite. In particular, the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture holds for curves.

Let φ:X→Y\varphi\colon X\to Y be a finite morphism of smooth curves and let y∈Yy\in Y. If φ∗​{y}=∑j=1kej​{xj}\varphi^{*}\{y\}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}e_{j}\{x_{j}\}, where ej≥ej′e_{j}\geq e_{j^{\prime}} for every j≤j′j\leq j^{\prime} and where all xjx_{j} are pairwise distinct, then we call the sequence λ=(e1,…,ek)\lambda=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k}) the ramification profile of yy. If yiy_{i} for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n is a numeration of all branching points of φ\varphi and λi\lambda_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n are their ramification profiles then we call (λ1,…,λn)(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) the ramification profile of φ\varphi (over the ordered branching locus (y1,…,yn)(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})).

Lemma 2.2 (Branched self-covers of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}; [Tho65]).

For a positive integer nn let Λ=(λ1,…,λn)\Lambda=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}), where λi=(λi,1,…,λi,ki)\lambda_{i}=(\lambda_{i,1},\ldots,\lambda_{i,k_{i}}), i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n are non-increasing sequences of positive integers with λi,1≥1\lambda_{i,1}\geq 1, and let y1,…,yky_{1},\ldots,y_{k} be distinct points in 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. Then a finite morphism φ:𝔸1→𝔸1\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{1} with ramification profile Λ\Lambda and branching locus (y1,…,yn)(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) exists if and only if there exists a positive integer dd, such that the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    λi,1+…+λi,ki=d\lambda_{i,1}+\ldots+\lambda_{i,k_{i}}=d for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

  2. (2)

    k1+k2+…+kn=(n−1)​d+1k_{1}+k_{2}+\ldots+k_{n}=(n-1)d+1.

The necessity of conditions is easy to see. The first one is satisfied with d=deg⁡φd=\deg\varphi as a consequence of the finiteness of φ\varphi. Since et​o​p​(𝔸1)=1e_{top}(\mathbb{A}^{1})=1, the second one follows from the Riemann-Hurwitz formula:

1=d⋅1−∑i,j(λi,j−1)=d−∑i(d−ki)=∑iki−(n−1)​d.1=d\cdot 1-\sum_{i,j}(\lambda_{i,j}-1)=d-\sum_{i}(d-k_{i})=\sum_{i}k_{i}-(n-1)d.

If X→ℙ1X\to\mathbb{P}^{1} is a branched cover with at most three branching points, say 0,1,∞0,1,\infty, then the inverse image of the interval [0,1][0,1] cuts XX into topologically contractible pieces and has a natural structure of a bi-colored graph with vertices being inverse images of 0,10,1 and with adjacent vertices of different colors. A graph of the latter type is called a dessin on XX, see [GGD12, §4] for details.

Proposition 2.3 (Dessin d’enfant, [GGD12], Proposition 4.20).

Let XX be a smooth projective curve. The above assignment induces a bijection between isomorphy classes of branched coverings X→ℙ1X\to\mathbb{P}^{1} with at most three ordered branching points and classes of dessins on XX modulo orientation-preserving homeomorphism of XX whose restriction induces an isomorphism between the bi-colored graphs.

We will be especially interested in branched self-covers of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} with at most 22 branching points. In this case X=ℙ1X=\mathbb{P}^{1} and the equivalence of branched covering is simply an automorphism of the source ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} fixing ∞\infty, hence an affine function. Such branched self-covers correspond to the so-called Belyi-Shabat polynomials, which are polynomials with at most two critical values (values at points in which the differential vanishes). These are extensively studied, in particular because the absolute Galois group Gal⁡(ℚ¯/ℚ)\operatorname{Gal}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}) acts faithfully on them (see [GGD12, Theorem 4.49]), and hence on planar bi-colored graphs (cf. Proposition 2.3). Some of the simplest Belyi-Shabat polynomials are the well-known Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kind. We call a critical point non-degenerate if its ramification index equals 22.

Example 2.4 (Chebyshev polynomials).

The nn-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind Tn​(x)∈ℂ​[x]T_{n}(x)\in\mathbb{C}[x] is defined by

Tn​(x)=2​x​Tn−1​(x)−Tn−2​(x)T_{n}(x)=2xT_{n-1}(x)-T_{n-2}(x)

where T0=1T_{0}=1 and T1​(x)=xT_{1}(x)=x. It is the unique polynomial satisfying Tn​(cos⁡x)=cos⁡n​xT_{n}(\cos x)=\cos nx. Its critical values are contained in {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. It follows that Tn​(−x)=(−1)n​Tn​(x)T_{n}(-x)=(-1)^{n}T_{n}(x) and Tn​(1)=1T_{n}(1)=1. The first few Chebyshev polynomials are T2​(x)=2​x2−1T_{2}(x)=2x^{2}-1, T3​(x)=4​x3−3​xT_{3}(x)=4x^{3}-3x, T4​(x)=8​x4−8​x2+1T_{4}(x)=8x^{4}-8x^{2}+1, T5​(x)=16​x5−20​x3+5​xT_{5}(x)=16x^{5}-20x^{3}+5x.

They are the unique polynomials satisfying Un−1​(cos⁡x)=sin⁡n​x/sin⁡xU_{n-1}(\cos x)=\sin nx/\sin x. It follows that Un−1​(±1)=(±1)n−1​nU_{n-1}(\pm 1)=(\pm 1)^{n-1}n.

Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kind satisfy the relation

(2.1) Tn2​(x)−1=(x2−1)​Un−12​(x).T_{n}^{2}(x)-1=(x^{2}-1)U_{n-1}^{2}(x).
Lemma 2.5 (Characterization of Chebyshev polynomials).

Let P⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[x]P(x)\in\mathbb{C}[x] be a polynomial with non-degenerate critical points and with ±1\pm 1 as the only critical values. Assume that ±1\pm 1 are not critical points, that P⁡(1)=1P(1)=1 and that P​(−1)2=1P(-1)^{2}=1. Then PP is a Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind.

We treat PP as a self-cover of ℙ1=𝔸1∪{∞}\mathbb{P}^{1}=\mathbb{A}^{1}\cup\{\infty\}. The assumption that the critical points are non-degenerate implies that the bi-colored graph associated with PP (see the discussion preceding Proposition 2.3) is a chain. The critical values are ±1\pm 1, so changing PP to −P-P if necessary we may assume that there is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of (ℙ1,∞)(\mathbb{P}^{1},\infty) identifying the bi-colored graphs of PP and of the Chebyshev polynomial TnT_{n}. By Proposition 2.3 branched self-coverings of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} induced by ±P\pm P and TnT_{n} are isomorphic via an isomorphism respecting ∞\infty, so ±P⁡(x)=Tn​(a​x+b)\pm P(x)=T_{n}(ax+b) for some a∈ℂ∗,b∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C}^{*},b\in\mathbb{C}. Since Tn​(−x)=(−1)n​T​(x)T_{n}(-x)=(-1)^{n}T(x), we may assume a>0a>0. The normalization conditions give {−a+b,a+b}⊆{−1,1}\{-a+b,a+b\}\subseteq\{-1,1\}, hence b=0b=0 and a=1a=1. Then P=±TnP=\pm T_{n}, so in fact P=TnP=T_{n}, because TnT_{n} and PP agree on x=1x=1. ∎

2B. Rational fibrations and completions.

By a fibration of an algebraic variety we mean a faithfully flat (hence surjective) morphism whose general fibers are irreducible, reduced and have positive dimension. A completion of a fibration ρ:S→B\rho\colon S\to B of a smooth variety is a triple (S¯,ι,ρ¯)(\bar{S},\iota,\bar{\rho}) consisting of a smooth complete variety S¯\bar{S}, an embedding ι:S→S¯\iota\colon S\to\bar{S} for which D=S¯∖SD=\bar{S}\setminus S is a simple normal crossing divisor and a fibration ρ¯:S¯→B¯\bar{\rho}\colon\bar{S}\to\bar{B}, where B¯\bar{B} is a smooth completion of BB, such that ρ¯|S=ρ\bar{\rho}|_{S}=\rho. In fact we will often refer to (S¯,D,ρ¯)(\bar{S},D,\bar{\rho}) as the completion, the identification S≅S¯∖DS\cong\bar{S}\setminus D being implicitly fixed. A completion is called minimal if it does not properly dominate other completions.

Definition 2.6.

If ρi:Si→Bi\rho_{i}\colon S_{i}\to B_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 are fibrations of varieties then we say that a morphism η:S1→S2\eta\colon S_{1}\to S_{2} respects the fibrations ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} if there exists a morphism φ:B1→B2\varphi\colon B_{1}\to B_{2} such that ρ2∘η=φ∘ρ1\rho_{2}\circ\eta=\varphi\circ\rho_{1}:

A fibration ρ:S→B\rho\colon S\to B of a normal surface SS is called a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}- or 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}- or an 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}-fibration if its general fibers are isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, 𝔸1=𝔸ℂ1\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}} or 𝔸∗1=𝔸ℂ1∖{0}\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}=\mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{0\} respectively. For such a fibration a fiber is called degenerate if it is not isomorphic to a general fiber, equivalently it is either non-reduced or its reduced form is not isomorphic to the general fiber. Fibers of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibrations of smooth projective surfaces are well understood. There are no multiple fibers and every reducible fiber contains a (−1)(-1)-curve which meets at most two other components of the fiber, so iterated contractions of such curves map the fiber onto a smooth 00-curve. In particular, every such fiber is a tree of rational curves. An 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}-fibration is untwisted if its generic fiber is 𝔸K,∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{K,*}, where K=ℂ⁡(B)K=\mathbb{C}(B), and twisted otherwise. Fibers of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}- and 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}-fibrations of affine surfaces can be easily described. By μ𝔸1∪{0}ν𝔸1\mu\mathbb{A}^{1}\cup_{\{0\}}\nu\mathbb{A}^{1} we denote the scheme Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y]/(xμ​yν))\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y]/(x^{\mu}y^{\nu})), which is a sum of two multiple affine lines whose reduced forms meet transversally at one point.

Notation 2.7.

For a curve CC contracted by a given fibration ρ:S→B\rho:S\to B of a surface we denote by μ⁡(C)\mu(C) the multiplicity of CC in the scheme-theoretic fiber of ρ\rho containing CC.

Lemma 2.8 (𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-, 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}-fibrations, [Miy01], 3.1.4.2, 3.1.7.3).

Let FF and Fg​e​nF_{gen} denote respectively a degenerate and a general fiber of a fibration of a smooth affine surface.

  1. (1)

    If Fg​e​n≅𝔸1F_{gen}\cong\mathbb{A}^{1} then Fred≅⨆i=1r𝔸1F_{\mathrm{red}}\cong\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb{A}^{1} for some r≥1r\geq 1.

  2. (2)

    If Fg​e​n≅𝔸∗1F_{gen}\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*} then Fred≅Γ⊔⨆i=1r𝔸1F_{\mathrm{red}}\cong\Gamma\sqcup\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb{A}^{1} for some r≥0r\geq 0 and Γ∈{∅\Gamma\in\{\emptyset, 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}, 𝔸1∪{0}𝔸1}\mathbb{A}^{1}\cup_{\{0\}}\mathbb{A}^{1}\}. Any two lines constituting a connected component with reduced form 𝔸1∪{0}𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}\cup_{\{0\}}\mathbb{A}^{1} have coprime multiplicities.

The only statement not proven in the above references is the one about multiplicities in (2). Deleting connected components whose reduced form is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} we may assume that r=0r=0. Let F¯\bar{F} be the fiber of the minimal completion of the fibration which contains FF and let G1,G2G_{1},G_{2} be the closures of the components of FF. The boundary DD of the completion is connected, because the initial surface is affine. We may assume μ⁡(G1),μ⁡(G2)≥2\mu(G_{1}),\mu(G_{2})\geq 2, hence G1+G2G_{1}+G_{2} does not meet sections contained in DD. The minimality implies that D∩F¯D\cap\bar{F} contains no (−1)(-1)-curves, and hence F¯\bar{F}, which is a tree of rational curves, contains a unique (−1)(-1)-curve, say G1G_{1}. The difference F¯∖F\bar{F}\setminus F has exactly two connected components, each meeting one of the sections contained in DD, hence containing a component of multiplicity 11. It follows that F¯\bar{F} is a chain of rational curves. By induction we argue that any two components of F¯\bar{F} which meet have coprime multiplicities. ∎

2C. ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes of negative Kodaira dimension and ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-pseudo-planes.

A ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane is a smooth complex surface whose Betti numbers are the same as those of the affine plane, that is, trivial in positive dimensions. As mentioned in the introduction, every ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane is affine. These surfaces are important for many problems in affine geometry and the attempts to fully understand them motivated lots of progress (see [Miy07], [Miy01, §3.4] and [Pal11] for a review). We need the following more detailed description (see [Miy01, §3.4] and [Fuj82, 5.9, 4.19]). By κ\kappa we denote the logarithmic Kodaira dimension. Cyclic groups are denoted by ℤm:=ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbb{Z}_{m}:=\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z} and the free product of groups by ∗*.

Lemma 2.9 (ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes with κ=−∞\kappa=-\infty).

A ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane SS of negative Kodaira dimension has an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:S→B\rho:S\to B, and for every such fibration the base curve BB and the reduced forms of all the fibers are isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}.

If μ1​F1,…,μn​Fn\mu_{1}F_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n}F_{n}, with FiF_{i} reduced, are all the degenerate fibers of ρ:S→B\rho:S\to B, then π1​(S)≅ℤμ1∗…∗ℤμn.\pi_{1}(S)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{\mu_{1}}*\ldots*\mathbb{Z}_{\mu_{n}}. In particular, π1​(S)\pi_{1}(S) is finite if and only if it is cyclic.

A ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane is called a pseudo-plane if it has negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension and a cyclic fundamental group. The following positive result concerning the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture was proved in [GM99, §3, §6]. Some simplifications and a correction of Theorem 6.2 from loc. cit. (the counterexample in case π1​(S)≅ℤ2∗ℤ2\pi_{1}(S)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\mathbb{Z}_{2}) were made in [Miy03, 2.4.3(2), 2.3.11].

Proposition 2.10 (GJC for ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes with κ=−∞\kappa=-\infty).

Let SS be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane of negative Kodaira dimension with a non-cyclic fundamental group. Then SS has a unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration and every étale endomorphism of SS respects it. Furthermore, the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture holds for SS, unless π1​(S)=ℤ2∗ℤ2\pi_{1}(S)=\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\mathbb{Z}_{2}.

Recall that a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action on a smooth surface S=Spec⁡(A)S=\operatorname{Spec}(A) is called hyperbolic if for every fixed point the weights of the induced linear action on the tangent space are non-zero and have different sign. Equivalently (see [KF91]), every fixed point is isolated and is not a limit point of every nearby orbit. For such actions, the algebraic quotient morphism ρ:S→S/ℂ∗=Spec⁡(Aℂ∗)\rho\colon S\to S/\mathbb{C}^{*}=\operatorname{Spec}(A^{\mathbb{C}^{*}}) is an 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}-fibration over a smooth curve.

We now review the description of pseudo-planes which admit hyperbolic ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-actions. We begin with their universal covers.

For fixed integers k,r≥1k,r\geq 1, the smooth affine surface

(2.2) S~(k,r)={xry=zk−1}⊆Spec(ℂ[x,y,z])\tilde{S}(k,r)=\{x^{r}y=z^{k}-1\}\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z])

Lemma 2.13 (Characterization of S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a), [MM06], [FZ06]).

Let SS be a non-trivial (S≇𝔸2S\not\cong\mathbb{A}^{2}) pseudo-plane with a hyperbolic ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action. Let k=|π1​(S)|k=|\pi_{1}(S)| and let rr be the maximal multiplicity of a fiber component of the quotient morphism isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. If r≥2r\geq 2 then there exists a∈{1,…,k−1}a\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\} coprime with kk such that SS is ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-equivariantly isomorphic to S⁡(k,r,a)S(k,r,a) with the ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action induced from (2.3). The isomorphism is unique up to a composition with the group automorphism λ↦λ−1\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-1} of ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}.

Since the ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action is hyperbolic, the quotient morphism is a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-fibration. Since S≇𝔸2S\not\cong\mathbb{A}^{2}, by Lemma 2.9 k≥2k\geq 2. From the above description we see that for r≥2r\geq 2 there is a smooth relatively minimal completion of the quotient morphism for which the boundary is not a rational chain, so by a theorem of Gizatullin [Giz71] SS has a unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. Then we infer the result from [MM06] and [FZ06]. ∎

Remark 2.14.

If an effective ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action on a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane is not hyperbolic then it is a linear action on 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}.

In general, if a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action on a smooth affine variety SS has an elliptic or a parabolic fixed point then by [Ryn92, Proposition 1.9] (which easily follows from [BH85]) SS is respectively either equivariantly isomorphic to some affine space with a linear ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action or it is a ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-vector bundle over the smooth quotient S/ℂ∗S/\mathbb{C}^{*}. In case SS is a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane the latter quotient is ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic, hence isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, so in both cases S≅𝔸2S\cong\mathbb{A}^{2} and the ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-action is linear. ∎

2D. Étale endomorphisms respecting fibrations.

Recall that a morphism f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y between varieties is called étale if it is flat and unramified. Since it is flat, it is open and equidimensional (all nonempty fibers of ff have the same dimension) and since it is also unramified, it is quasi-finite (its fibers are finite). Assume that XX and YY are smooth. If f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is dominant equidimensional then by [Mat89, 23.1] it is automatically flat. It follows from [Mum88, Cor. 2, §III.5] that ff is étale if and only if it is a local isomorphism in the complex topology, equivalently, if and only if the differential is an isomorphism for every point of XX.

For a quasi-finite morphism of smooth quasi-projective varieties f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y, the Zariski-Nagata purity theorem implies that the complement E⊂XE\subset X of the étale locus of ff is of pure codimension one. It supports an effective, canonically defined ramification divisor of ff, denoted by RfR_{f}, which is linearly equivalent to f∗​KY−KXf^{*}K_{Y}-K_{X}, see [Iit82, pp. 202]. The image of the ramification locus is called the branching locus.

Lemma 2.15 (Étale endomorphisms).

Let SS be a smooth variety and let η:S→S\eta\colon S\to S be étale.

  1. (1)

    For every reduced divisor DD on SS the divisor η∗​D\eta^{*}D is reduced.

  2. (2)

    If deg⁡η=1\deg\eta=1 then η\eta is invertible.

  3. (3)

    If η\eta is proper and et​o​p​(S)≠0e_{top}(S)\neq 0 then η\eta is invertible.

  4. (4)

    Let (S¯,D)(\overline{S},D) be a smooth completion of SS and let Φm:S¯⇢ℙm:=ℙ⁡(|m⁡(KS¯+D)|)\Phi_{m}\colon\overline{S}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}_{m}:=\mathbb{P}(|m(K_{\overline{S}}+D)|) be the mm-th log canonical map. Then Φm∘η=pm​(η)∘Φm\Phi_{m}\circ\eta=p_{m}(\eta)\circ\Phi_{m} for some pm​(η)∈Aut⁡ℙmp_{m}(\eta)\in\operatorname{Aut}\mathbb{P}_{m}.

  5. (5)

    A restriction of η\eta to a closed subvariety of SS is unramified. In particular, if ℓ⊆S\ell\subseteq S is isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} then η⁡(ℓ)\eta(\ell) has no unibranched singular points (no cusps) and η|ℓ\eta_{|\ell} has degree 11.

(1) This follows from the fact that η\eta is unramified, see e.g. [SGA71, Proposition I.3.2 and Definition I.3.2].

(2) If deg⁡η=1\deg\eta=1 then η\eta is an open embedding, hence an isomorphism by the Ax-Grothendieck theorem [GD66, Theorem 10.4.11].

(3) Since η\eta is étale, it has finite fibers, so being proper, it is finite by [GD66, Theorem 8.11.1]. Finite étale morphisms are covers in the complex topology, so we get et​o​p​(S)=deg⁡η⋅et​o​p​(S)e_{top}(S)=\deg\eta\cdot e_{top}(S), and hence deg⁡η=1\deg\eta=1. By (2) η\eta is invertible.

(4) See [Iit82, Propositon 11.9].

(5) The first statement follows from the fact that a closed immersion is unramified and that the composition of two unramified morphisms is unramified. Assume ℓ⊆S\ell\subseteq S is isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. Let η′:ℓ→ℓ′\eta^{\prime}\colon\ell\to\ell^{\prime} be the lift of η|ℓ\eta|_{\ell} to the normalization ℓ′\ell^{\prime} of η⁡(ℓ)\eta(\ell). Then κ⁡(ℓ′)≤κ⁡(ℓ)\kappa(\ell^{\prime})\leq\kappa(\ell), so ℓ′\ell^{\prime} is isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} or ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. But η′\eta^{\prime} is unramified, so it extends to a, necessarily finite, endomorphism of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} with at most one ramification point. By the Riemann-Hurwitz formula this endomorphism has degree 11, so η|ℓ\eta|_{\ell} has degree 11. ∎

Given a variety SS we denote the monoid of its étale endomorphisms by E´​t⁡(S)\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S).

Lemma 2.16 (Lift to the universal cover).

Let π:S~→S\pi\colon\tilde{S}\to S be a finite étale cover of smooth varieties. Assume S~\tilde{S} is simply connected. Then every η∈E´​t⁡(S)\eta\in\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S) lifts to some η~∈E´​t⁡(S~)\tilde{\eta}\in\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(\tilde{S}) such that π∘η~=η∘π\pi\circ\tilde{\eta}=\eta\circ\pi. In particular, deg⁡η~=deg⁡η\deg\tilde{\eta}=\deg\eta, so η∈Aut⁡(S)\eta\in\operatorname{Aut}(S) if and only if η~∈Aut⁡(S~)\tilde{\eta}\in\operatorname{Aut}(\tilde{S}).

First recall that π\pi has the universal property that it factors through every finite étale cover f:X→Sf\colon X\to S of SS. Indeed the existence of a morphism πX:S~→X\pi_{X}\colon\tilde{S}\to X such that π=f∘πX\pi=f\circ\pi_{X} is equivalent to the existence of a section of the projection S~×SX→S~\tilde{S}\times_{S}X\to\tilde{S}. But the latter, being a pullback of ff, is a finite étale cover of S~\tilde{S}, so since S~\tilde{S} is simply connected, it is a trivial cover, which therefore admits a section. Let now (S′,η′,π′)(S^{\prime},\eta^{\prime},\pi^{\prime}) be the fiber product of η\eta and π\pi. Then η′:S′→S~\eta^{\prime}\colon S^{\prime}\to\tilde{S} is étale of degree deg⁡η′=deg⁡η\deg\eta^{\prime}=\deg\eta while π′:S′→S\pi^{\prime}\colon S^{\prime}\to S is étale and finite, of degree deg⁡π′=deg⁡π\deg\pi^{\prime}=\deg\pi. By the universal property of π\pi, there exists a morphism α:S~→S′\alpha\colon\tilde{S}\to S^{\prime} such that π′∘α=π\pi^{\prime}\circ\alpha=\pi, and then η~=η′∘α\tilde{\eta}=\eta^{\prime}\circ\alpha is as required. ∎

Notation 2.17.

If ρ:S→B\rho\colon S\to B is a fibration of algebraic varieties and an étale endomorphism η\eta of SS respects ρ\rho then by Definition 2.6, there exists an endomorphism ηρ:B→B\eta_{\rho}\colon B\to B, such that ρ∘η=ηρ∘ρ\rho\circ\eta=\eta_{\rho}\circ\rho. We denote by E´​t⁡(S,ρ)\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S,\rho) the submonoid of E´​t⁡(S)\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S) consisting of étale endomorphisms respecting ρ\rho.

The following Lemma is a minor improvement of [GM99, 3.1].

Lemma 2.18 (Condition on multiplicities for étale endomorphisms).

Let ρi:Si→Bi\rho_{i}\colon S_{i}\to B_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 be fibrations of smooth surfaces over smooth curves and let η:S1→S2\eta\colon S_{1}\to S_{2} be an endomorphism respecting ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2}, with the induced morphism φ:B1→B2\varphi\colon B_{1}\to B_{2}. Let e⁡(φ,p)e(\varphi,p) denote the ramification index of φ\varphi at p∈B1p\in B_{1}. If η\eta is étale then for every irreducible curve CC contracted by ρ1\rho_{1} we have

(2.8) μ⁡(η⁡(C))=e⁡(φ,ρ⁡(C))⋅μ⁡(C).\mu(\eta(C))=e(\varphi,\rho(C))\cdot\mu(C).

Conversely, if (2.8) holds for every irreducible curve CC contracted by ρ1\rho_{1} and η\eta is étale on general fibers of ρ1\rho_{1} then η\eta is étale.

Let C1C_{1} be an irreducible curve contracted by ρ1\rho_{1}. Put C2=η⁡(C1)C_{2}=\eta(C_{1}), pi=ρi​(Ci)p_{i}=\rho_{i}(C_{i}) and e=e⁡(φ,p1)e=e(\varphi,p_{1}). Write η∗​(C2)=m​C1+R\eta^{*}(C_{2})=mC_{1}+R for some m≥1m\geq 1 and an effective divisor RR contained in fibers and not containing C1C_{1}. Since η∗∘ρ2∗​(p2)=ρ1∗∘φ∗​(p2)\eta^{*}\circ\rho_{2}^{*}(p_{2})=\rho_{1}^{*}\circ\varphi^{*}(p_{2}), looking at the coefficient of C1C_{1} in the latter divisor we get

(2.9) μ⁡(C2)​m=e​μ​(C1).\mu(C_{2})m=e\mu(C_{1}).

If η\eta is étale then m=1m=1 by 2.15(1), which gives (2.8). For the converse implication, we note that since η\eta is quasi-finite, it is flat by [Mat89, 23.1]. Because S1S_{1} is smooth, the Zariski-Nagata purity theorem implies that the ramification locus of η\eta is either empty or has pure codimension 11. But by (2.8) m=1m=1 for every C1C_{1} as above, so the ramification divisor has no components contained in fibers. By assumption η\eta is étale along general fibers of ρ1\rho_{1}, hence the ramification divisor of η\eta is trivial. ∎

Example 2.19.

Let BB, CC be smooth curves and let ηC\eta_{C} be a dominating endomorphism of CC. Then η=idB×ηC\eta=\operatorname{id}_{B}\times\eta_{C} is an endomorphism of (B×C,prB)(B\times C,\operatorname{pr}_{B}) which trivially satisfies (2.8) and which is étale if and only if ηC\eta_{C} is étale. Note that if C≠𝔸1,ℙ1C\neq\mathbb{A}^{1},\mathbb{P}^{1} then κ⁡(C)≥0\kappa(C)\geq 0, so by [Iit82, Theorem 11.7] every dominating endomorphism of CC is automatically étale. On the other hand, dominating endomorphisms of degee at least 22 are never étale for C=𝔸1,ℙ1C=\mathbb{A}^{1},\mathbb{P}^{1}.

Lemma 2.20 (One non-reduced fiber).

Let SS be a smooth surface equipped with a fibration ρ:S→B\rho\colon S\to B with at most one non-reduced fiber. Then every η∈E´​t⁡(S,ρ)\eta\in\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S,\rho) induces a (finite) étale endomorphism of BB.

By Lemma 2.1 ηρ\eta_{\rho} is finite. Suppose that ηρ:B→B\eta_{\rho}\colon B\to B has ramification index d>1d>1 at some point p∈Bp\in B. By [Iit82, Prop. 11.7] B≅𝔸1B\cong\mathbb{A}^{1} or ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Let q=ηρ​(p)q=\eta_{\rho}(p) and for any u∈Bu\in B put Fu=ρ∗​(u)F_{u}=\rho^{*}(u). By definition ηρ∗​(q)−d​p\eta_{\rho}^{*}(q)-dp is effective, hence ρ∗​(ηρ∗​(q)−d​p)=η∗​(ρ∗​(q))−d​ρ∗​(p)=η∗​(Fq)−d​Fp\rho^{*}(\eta_{\rho}^{*}(q)-dp)=\eta^{*}(\rho^{*}(q))-d\rho^{*}(p)=\eta^{*}(F_{q})-dF_{p} is effective, so η∗​(Fq)\eta^{*}(F_{q}) is a non-reduced divisor and, because η\eta is étale, the fiber FqF_{q} is non-reduced by Lemma 2.15(1). So if ρ\rho has no multiple fiber then we are done. Otherwise, FqF_{q} must be the unique non-reduced fiber of ρ\rho. 3. Proof of Theorem A. Reduction to ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}-actions.

In this section we prove Theorem A in case G=ℂ+G=\mathbb{C}^{+}, that is, we prove the ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant Jacobian Conjecture for ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes of negative Kodaira dimension.

Notation 3.1.

3B. ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant GJC holds.

Proposition 3.3 (ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant GJC).

The ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant Generalized Jacobian Conjecture holds for ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes with an effective ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}action.

Let SS be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane with an effective ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-action Λt:S→S\Lambda_{t}\colon S\to S, t∈ℂ+t\in\mathbb{C}^{+}. Suppose η∈E´​tℂ+⁡(S)\eta\in\operatorname{\acute{E}t}_{\mathbb{C}^{+}}(S) is non-proper and put n=deg⁡η>1n=\deg\eta>1. The quotient morphism is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:S→Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x])\rho\colon S\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x]) respected by η\eta. By Proposition 3.2 SS is not a pseudo-plane, ρ\rho has exactly two degenerate fibers and there is a birational morphism σ:S→𝔸2\sigma\colon S\to\mathbb{A}^{2} such that ρ=pr1∘σ\rho=\operatorname{pr}_{1}\circ\sigma and an endomorphism η0∈End⁡(𝔸2,pr1)\eta_{0}\in\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{A}^{2},\operatorname{pr}_{1}) given by

η0​(x,y)=(Tn​(x),A⁡(x)​y+B⁡(x)),\eta_{0}(x,y)=(T_{n}(x),A(x)y+B(x)),

where A=Un−12​aA=U^{2}_{n-1}a, B=(x2−1)​Un−1​bB=(x^{2}-1)U_{n-1}b, and where a,b∈ℂ⁡[x]a,b\in\mathbb{C}[x] and A⁡(1)=±nA(1)=\pm n such that η0∘σ=σ∘η\eta_{0}\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ\eta.

We now derive a contradiction from the assumption that η\eta is ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant. First of all note that, in principle, a minimal ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant completion of ρ\rho can have a higher Picard rank than the minimal completion S¯\bar{S} used in the proof of Proposition 3.2. Thus S¯\bar{S} is a ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant smooth completion of SS. Then, since 11-dimensional orbits of a ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-action are necessarily isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}, we infer that the contractions σi\sigma_{i} of (−1)(-1)-curves contained in fibers are ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant, so the diagram (3.2) is ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant.

3C. Miyanishi’s counterexample expanded.

Let again SS be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology plane with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:S→𝔸1\rho\colon S\to\mathbb{A}^{1}. If η\eta is a non-proper étale endomorphism of SS respecting ρ\rho (hence a counterexample to the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture for SS) then by Proposition 3.2 π1​(S)≅ℤ2∗ℤ2\pi_{1}(S)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\mathbb{Z}_{2}. A first example of this type has been constructed by Miyanishi [Miy03, 2.4.3(2), 2.3.11]; it has degree 22. We now make a digression to show how our computations from the previous section can be applied to construct counterexamples of any degree. Note that by Proposition 3.3 η\eta is not ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-equivariant for any effective ℂ+\mathbb{C}^{+}-action on SS.

Example 3.4 (Miyanishi’s ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic counterexample with π1=ℤ2∗ℤ2\pi_{1}=\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\mathbb{Z}_{2}).

Let (C,p−1,p1,p∞)(C,p_{-1},p_{1},p_{\infty}) be a plane conic with a triple of distinct points on it. In [Miy03, 2.4.3(2), 2.3.11] Miyanishi argues geometrically that SS has an étale endomorphism of degree 22. Namely, let (S′,ρ′,φ′)(S^{\prime},\rho^{\prime},\varphi^{\prime}) be the normalized pullback of ρ:S→𝔸1\rho\colon S\to\mathbb{A}^{1} and φ:𝔸1→𝔸1\varphi\colon\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{1} given by φ⁡(x)=2​x2−1\varphi(x)=2x^{2}-1. If we remove from S′S^{\prime} one of the components of the latter fiber then one shows that we get a surface isomorphic with SS. We now complete the proof of Theorem A.

Let η∈E´​tG⁡(S)∖Aut⁡(S)\eta\in\operatorname{\acute{E}t}_{G}(S)\setminus\operatorname{Aut}(S). Suppose the action is not hyperbolic. By Remark 2.14 it is the action λ⋅(x,y)→(λp​x,λq​y)\lambda\cdot(x,y)\to(\lambda^{p}x,\lambda^{q}y) on 𝔸2=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y])\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y]) for some coprime integers p,q≥0p,q\geq 0. By Lemma 2.18 η~\tilde{\eta} is étale, so η∘π=π∘η~\eta\circ\pi=\pi\circ\tilde{\eta} is étale. Since π:S~→S\pi\colon\tilde{S}\to S is surjective and étale, η~\tilde{\eta} is étale. ∎

Remark 4.2.
  1. (1)

    Our counterexamples to the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture seem to be the first ones in literature which are simply connected and have negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension, and also the first ones which are simply connected and rational. Note that in [Miy03] the Remark on page 80 and the comment above Example 2.2.10 are incorrect. Indeed, in the first case the given endomorphism of {xrz+yd=1}\{x^{r}z+y^{d}=1\}, namely η⁡(x,y,z)=(x,yn,z⁡(1−yn​d)/(1−yd))\eta(x,y,z)=(x,y^{n},z(1-y^{nd})/(1-y^{d})), is not étale for y=0y=0. In the second case X~\widetilde{X} is not simply connected, as its fundamental group is ℤ2∗ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}*\mathbb{Z}_{2}.

  2. (2)

    It follows from Example 2.2.2 and Theorem 2.2.8 in [Miy03] that the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture fails for the triple cover of the complement of a smooth planar cubic. This is a simply connected surface with logarithmic Kodaira dimension equal to 00. This example leads also to a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-acyclic counterexample of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 00 (see Example 2.2.3(5) loc. cit.).

5B. Deformations of étale endomorphisms.

In this section we prove Theorem C. We denote by 𝔸∞\mathbb{A}^{\infty} the infinite affine space defined as the colimit of open immersions id𝔸n×{0}:𝔸n↪𝔸n×𝔸1=𝔸n+1\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}\times\{0\}\colon\mathbb{A}^{n}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathbb{A}^{n+1}, n≥1n\geq 1.

Notation 5.4.

Given a variety SS the automorphism group Aut⁡(S)\mathrm{Aut}(S) of SS acts on the monoid of étale endomorphisms E´​t⁡(S)\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S) by left and right compositions. We denote the set of double cosets Aut⁡(S)∖E´​t⁡(S)/Aut⁡(S){\mathrm{Aut}(S)\setminus}\!\operatorname{\acute{E}t}(S)\!{/\mathrm{Aut}(S)} of these actions by E´​C⁡(S)\operatorname{\acute{E}C}(S).

Recall that for every polynomial P∈ℂ⁡[x]P\in\mathbb{C}[x] the surface S~​(k,r)\tilde{S}(k,r) has an automorphism ΘP:=Θ1P\Theta^{P}:=\Theta^{P}_{1} (see Example 2.11) given by

(5.9) ΘP​(x,y,z):=Θ1P​(x,y,z)=(x,y+x−r​((z+P⁡(x)​xr)k−zk),z+P⁡(x)​xr).\Theta^{P}(x,y,z):=\Theta^{P}_{1}(x,y,z)=(x,y+x^{-r}((z+P(x)x^{r})^{k}-z^{k}),z+P(x)x^{r}).

Combining it with the factorization obtained in Corollary 5.2 we obtain the following result, which establishes Theorem C.

Proposition 5.5 (Family of étale endomorphisms).

Write η=π∘jη\eta=\pi\circ j_{\eta} for jη:S→S~​(k,r¯​k)j_{\eta}\colon S\to\tilde{S}(k,\bar{r}k) as in Lemma 5.1. Then the map Ωη:𝔸∞→E´​C⁡(S)\Omega_{\eta}\colon\mathbb{A}^{\infty}\to\operatorname{\acute{E}C}(S) defined by
